newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia Gas Oil/Jet - Gas oil steady despite crude.
newsitem.headline: Asia Gas Oil/Jet - Gas oil steady despite crude.

text.p: Singapore gas oil edged up slightly despite a big jump to overnight crude values as the market continued to be weighed down by ample supplies against strong support at the $25.00 level, traders said on Friday.
Traders said the market is range bound because of some traders' willingness to buy all cargoes offered below $25.50 per barrel but not bidding above this price.
The three traders who are buying have bought more than 19 million barrels of gas oil since the start of March 3.
Two 150,000-barrel cargoes traded, a Swiss trader sold to a local trader at $25.00 per barrel for May 24-28 lifting and a European major sold to the same local trader at $25.40 for June 4-8 lifting.
Jet fuel extended its latest slip as refiners continue to offer the market down in the absence of fresh regional enduser demand.
The refiners had over the week found a welcome buyer in the form of a local trader who has this week bought 500,000 barrels of jet fuel.

A European major sold the cargoes at $24.80 per barrel for May 26-30 lifting and at $25.10 for June 4-8 lifting, down between 10 cents from Thursday's traded level for the May cargo with the June cargo traded unchanged.
As a result of the lower offers, the regrade slipped with June last quoted at 20/40 cents compared to 40/50 cents on Thursday, brokers said.
Market attention was slightly diverted by the unexpectedly low offers in to India's one-year term tender to buy high speed diesel for delivery from June 1997 to May 1998.

Traders said the lowest offer came from a Japanese trader for the delivery of 140,000 tonnes to Kandla on the west coast at 68 cents per tonne over Middle East quotes, on a cost-and-freight basis (c-and-f).

Next was from a Middle East producer for the delivery of 80,000 tonnes at around 90 cents premium with the same Japanese trader offering at about 6 cents above this for 87,000 tonne cargoes, both above MidEast quotes on a c-and-f basis.
Low offers were also seen for the normal 45,000-tonne lots which were heard at around $2.00 premium c-and-f Kandla, about 50 cents below last year's awarded price.
Industry sources said the low offers were due to market perception that supplies will exceed demand over the next 12 months caused by capacity expansions in Asia and the Middle East.
"The numbers (premiums) just cover the freight costs, in some cases even that is not covered. These people are taking the long term view that the market will be in surplus," said a trader.
Most industry sources said that IOC is very likely to take only one of the large cargoes offered.
The tender closes on May 14.
